cue: The view is wide and blurry, and it runs slowly, then jumps ahead.
rows: Most insects see less than a sixtieth as much detail as people do.
Flies and dragonflies can see a light flicker more than 100 times a second, and one beetle up to 400. People stop at about 60. This view runs slowly and then jumps ahead to suggest the difference.
Bees and some other insects can see ultraviolet light, which people can’t. Phone cameras capture very little of it, so the violet tint in this view stands in for it.

src: research/insect evidence L1 and L190 to L192: van der Kooi and Stavenga 2021 (most insects studied have ultraviolet, blue and green receptors; the peaks are the seven-spot ladybird's, 360, 420 and 520 nm)

rows: Most insects see less than a sixtieth as much detail as people do.
Flies and dragonflies can see a light flicker more than 100 times a second, and one beetle up to 400. People stop at about 60. This view runs slowly and then jumps ahead to suggest the difference.
Bees and some other insects can see ultraviolet light, which people can’t. Phone cameras capture very little of it, so the violet tint in this view stands in for it.
On this trial the colours come from the measured receptor peaks (360, 420, 520 nm). The camera's colours and the display are the app's.

Many insects see the direction in which sky light is polarized, strongest in a band 90 degrees from the sun, and steer by it. With &draw=polar and the motion sensors on, fine strokes show that band from the time, the date and the phone's heading. The latitude is taken as 35 degrees north, and the drawing is the app's.

polar.note: how strongly the polarized band of sky is drawn
